title: Building the beer list
lead: How a good list is organized, labeled, rotated and kept fresh.

sections.name: Organize by flavor
know: Group by taste (crisp, roasty, hoppy), not country.
Give staff enough to describe beers they haven’t tried.
97% of craft drinkers say flavor matters (BA, 2015).
sections.source: FSR Magazine, “Anatomy of a Beer List”; Brewers Association / CraftBeer.com, Beer & Food Course

video.title: Craft Beer’s Place on the Menu

keyPoints.line: of craft drinkers rate flavor important.

read.bigIdea: A list is a menu of flavors.
read.where: Organize by **flavor**, not by country: region doesn’t tell a guest how a beer tastes. One DC restaurant group uses headings like **Crisp**, **Roast**, **Tart & Funky**, **Fruit and Spice**, **Hop**. Give each beer a **category, style and key ingredients**, so staff can describe one they haven’t tasted yet. In a 2015 Nielsen poll for the Brewers Association, **97%** of craft drinkers rated **flavor** important when ordering.
read.mixup: Very specific style headings please experts and confuse everyone else.

read.where: Put **ABV** next to the **pour size**. A US **standard drink** is about 0.6 oz of pure alcohol: **12 oz of 5%** beer. So **12 oz of a 10%** beer is **two** drinks, and a 16 oz pour of 8% is about two. Label NA beer the federal way: **non-alcoholic** means **under 0.5%** ABV (with that statement), **alcohol-free** means none, and **low** or **reduced alcohol** means under 2.5%.
read.mixup: “Non-alcoholic” isn’t zero. For a guest who can’t have any alcohol, offer an alcohol-free one.
read.sayIt: That one’s 9%, so we pour it in a smaller glass.

video.title: The Tulip Glass | The Beer Heads - Glassware 101

keyPoints.line: the one glass if you only have one.

read.bigIdea: A list is only as good as its freshest beer.
read.where: If you can only stock one beer glass, the Brewers Association suggests a **16 oz footed tulip** (it calls the shaker pint a mixing glass). Plan **tap rotations** so no keg sits past **45 days**, and give cider and flavored beers **their own lines**. Cicerone expects the program to sell in **date order**, pull out-of-date beer, and train staff to sell **every** beer on the list so nothing ages in the cooler.
read.mixup: A long list isn’t a better list if half of it sits in the cooler going stale.

sections.name: Off beer and the cellar list

video.title: Should I age my beer? | The Craft Beer Channel

keyPoints.line: aging beer before you list it.

read.where: When a beer tastes off: **pull it** from draft or inventory, keep back-stock cold, take it **off the menu**, tell staff, then call the **distributor** (and the brewery if needed). Staff should know a flawed beer from one they just don’t like. For a **cellar list**, the three S’s age well: **strong** (about 8%+), **sour** and **smoked**. Check with the brewery, **taste** after six months and then yearly, and list it when it’s ready.
read.mixup: Aged beer can sell at a premium, but the restaurant carries the risk if it fades.

sources: FSR Magazine; Brewers Association / CraftBeer.com, Beer & Food Course; NIH/NIAAA, “What Is a Standard Drink?”; US Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, malt beverage labeling rules; Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual, 4th ed., 2019 (brewersassociation.org); Cicerone, Advanced Cicerone Syllabus v6.0 and exam page (cicerone.org). Checked Nov 8, 2026.
